Spine fractures account for only 2% to 5% of all pediatric fractures but may result in
considerable disability and mortality.
Many unique considerations for pathophysiology, diagnosis, and treatment in pediatric
patients
Injuries to other organ systems occur in 40% to 50% of children with a spinal injury.
Motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) are the most common mechanism of injury across all age
groups.

Overview
Spine injuries in pediatric and adolescent patients are potentially devastating injuries,
with a 16% to 18% mortality rate, a 20% to 35% risk of neurologic deficit from cervical
fractures,1-3 and a 3% to 5% overall mortality rate4,5 (Resource 1). The mortality rate is
considerably higher in pediatric patients than in adults, associated with an increased
likelihood of cervical spine injury because of a larger head-to-body ratio, hyperlaxity in
the cervical spine, and a high rate of concomitant head injury associated with upper
cervical spine injuries.1,3,6-8 Although the management of spine injuries largely has been
extrapolated from the adult literature, some unique features are present in the pediatric
population with regard to pathophysiology of, evaluation of, diagnosis of, and surgical
and nonsurgical management for cervical (Resource 2) and thoracolumbar (Resource 3)
spine injuries.
Epidemiology
The incidence of spine injury requiring hospitalization among all patients is less than 0.1%,
whereas the risk of spinal cord injury (SCI) is less than 0.01%.
In children younger than 11 years, higher risk of upper cervical spine injury
Adolescents 11 years or older are more likely to sustain adult-type injuries in the
thoracolumbar spine and/or subaxial cervical spine.


In a review of the Kids’ Inpatient Database and National Trauma Data Bank for children
hospitalized in the United States, the overall incidence of spine injury in pediatric
patients is approximately 100 per 1 million pediatric individuals, whereas the incidence
of SCI is 20 per 1 million pediatric individuals. The incidence of spine injury has been
trending downward in the past decade;9 however, this number may be underestimated
because of on-scene mortality or death during transportation. The overall risk of a spine
injury is eight times higher in adolescents; however, the frequency of mortality and SCI in
young children is relatively increased because of the propensity for upper cervical spine
ligamentous injuries.
In a multicenter study of level 1 trauma centers that evaluated 332 children and
adolescents with spinal trauma, 84% of all injuries occurred in the individuals aged 13 to
19 years.5 Of all the spine injuries, 36% of the fractures occurred in the cervical spine,
31% of the fractures occurred in the thoracic spine, and 51% of the fractures occurred in
the lumbar spine. In patients aged 0 to 3 years, more than 50% of patients had cervical
spine injury, with 83% having an injury at C3 or higher compared with only 37% of
patients aged 13 to 19 years. The overall mortality rate was 3.6%, and the incidence of
neurologic injury was 7%. Of all the neurologic injuries, 21 of 24 were SCIs, including 16
(76%) complete SCIs and 5 (24%) incomplete SCIs, and 3 of 24 (12.5%) were nerve root
injuries.5
As many as one-half of pediatric patients have multilevel contiguous injuries, and 6% to
9% have multilevel noncontiguous injuries.5,10,11 Equivalent frequency is noted between
sex in children younger than 11 years because most of these patients are injured in a
MVC or fall. In adolescents, prior studies noted an increased frequency in males, with a
1.6:1 ratio6 from MVCs and sports/recreational activities, whereas more recent studies
have reported equivalent frequency between males and females.5
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Children younger than 8 years have an increased risk of cervical spine injury because of a
larger head-to-body ratio, greater ligamentous laxity, and differences in osseous anatomy.


Anatomy and Biomechanics
Compared with normal spinal anatomy in adults, pediatric patients have characteristic
features of the developing spine. Differences exist in cervical and thoracolumbar
osseous structures and, tissue elasticity, and the presence of physes may predispose
pediatric patients to different types of injuries.
Osteology and Joints
Children have a larger head-to-body ratio than adolescents and adults, with a more cephalad
fulcrum of flexion.
Pediatric synchondroses often are confused with fractures1 (Figure 1), and cartilaginous end
plates may fracture in a manner similar to that of Salter-Harris type 1 fractures.
Pediatric cervical spine anatomy differs from adult cervical spine anatomy, allowing for greater
mobility in flexion and extension, which predisposes children younger than 11 years to upper
cervical spine injury.
Pediatric thoracolumbar anatomy, the iliac crest, and the rib cage are underdeveloped
compared with that in adults, predisposing pediatric patients to SCI and associated visceral
injuries.

(Reproduced from Copley LA, Dormans JP: Cervicla spine disorders in infants and children. J Am


Osteology and Joints
The atlas (C1) is composed of three ossification centers: a body and two lateral masses.
The anterior arch ossifies by age 1 year, whereas the posterior arch fuses between ages
3 to 4 years. The neurocentral synchondroses close between ages 6 to 8 years. The axis
(C2) is composed of five ossification centers (the body, two lateral masses, and two
halves of the dens) and a secondary ossification center at the tip of odontoid. The
dentocentral (or basilar) synchondrosis separates the odontoid from the body and is
located inferior to the superior articular facets; the dentocentral synchondrosis typically
fuses by age 7 years and is prone to fracture in younger patients. The subaxial cervical
spine (C3 through C7) vertebrae are composed of three ossification centers: a body and
two neural arches. The neural arches fuse posteriorly between ages 2 to 3 years,
whereas the neurocentral synchondroses fuse between ages 3 to 6 years.1

The cervical facet joints in pediatric patients are oriented relatively horizontal compared
with those in adults, which decreases stability and predisposes pediatric patients to
injury. The upper cervical facets increase from 30° at birth to 60° to 70° by adolescence,
whereas the lower cervical facets increase from 55° to 70°. In the developing spine, the
vertebral bodies are wedged-shaped with decreased anterior height in the sagittal plane,
and the uncinate processes are virtually absent in children younger than 10 years.4
As vertebral bodies lose their wedge-shaped configuration, facets transition to a more
vertical orientation and ligaments lose their hyperflexibility. As the atlas neurocentral
synchondrosis and the axis dentocentral synchondroses fuse, the fulcrum during spinal
flexion shifts caudally from C2-C3 in early childhood to C5-C6 by age 10 years,
contributing to the shift in injury pattern from upper cervical spine injuries in young
children to a more adult-type injury pattern in adolescents.1,12
In the thoracolumbar spine, the facets are more horizontal and shallow in young
children, predisposing them to injury. In addition, associated osseous structures,
including the ribs and iliac crest, are less developed, resulting in an increased risk for
spinal column injury and associated intra-abdominal and intrathoracic organ injuries.
Ligaments and Soft Tissue
Young pediatric patients have greater ligamentous laxity

Ligaments and Soft Tissue
Pediatric patients have greater flexibility and elasticity of the interspinous ligaments and
the posterior facet joint capsules. The nucleus pulposus has greater water content and
less collagen cross-linking, contributing to greater elasticity. In addition, the paraspinal
musculature is immature and underdeveloped, yielding decreased ability to dissipate
forces through the spinal column, which predisposes patients to injury. This relative

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000579
6/80

hyperlaxity contributes to injury patterns in patients younger than 8 years that differ
from those in adolescents and adults.1,2
Neural Anatomy
A discrepancy in the hypermobility of the pediatric spinal column relative to the inflexibility of
the spinal cord contributes to SCIs.

Neural Anatomy
The spinal cord ends at L3 in newborns and migrates cephalad during childhood to end
at L1 or L2 during adolescence. Although the immature spinal column can stretch as
much as 5 cm without rupture, the spinal cord ruptures at 5 to 6 mm of traction and,
therefore, may cause SCI without radiographic abnormalities (SCIWORA).4,13
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
MVCs are the most common cause of spinal injury among pediatric patients.
Nonaccidental trauma accounts for 40% of spine trauma in children aged 2 years or younger.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
MVCs are the most common mechanism of injury among young children and
adolescents. Motor vehicle versus bicycle collisions, and motor vehicle versus pedestrian
collisions are associated with multiple injuries and poor outcomes.6 MVCs that are
considered high risk include: head-on collision, rollover, ejection from the vehicle, death
in the same crash, or speed greater than 55 mph.
Nonaccidental trauma accounts for 40% of spine trauma in children aged 2 years or
younger.4 Upper cervical spine injuries are the most common and often are purely

ligamentous; however, multilevel injuries and other associated trauma are common.
Falls from greater than body height is the other main mechanism of injury in young
children.
Although most severe spine fractures in pediatric patients with associated SCI are
associated with high energy mechanisms of injury, the most common fractures in
patients aged 18 years or younger are thoracolumbar compression fractures secondary
to lower energy mechanisms of injury. In addition to MVCs, sports and other recreational
activities account for most spinal injuries in older children and adolescents. Almost 30%
of sports injuries are associated with football, whereas other high-risk activities include
diving, rugby, skiing, bicycling, and all-terrain vehicle (ATV) use. Penetrating injuries,
including gunshot wounds currently account for 5% of all injuries and 15% to 20% of SCIs
in pre-teens and teens.5,14
In a multicenter study of level 1 trauma centers evaluating 332 children and adolescents
with spinal trauma, Rush et al5 reported that 62% of injuries resulted from a MVC, 9% of
injuries resulted from an ATV accident, 6% of injuries resulted from a fall, 5% of injuries
resulted from a gunshot wound, and 3% of injuries resulted from a motor vehicle versus
pedestrian collision. Nonaccidental trauma accounted for 1.4% of patients overall;
however, nonaccidental trauma was the reported mechanism of injury in 20% of patients
aged 3 years or younger. Of the children who sustained an injury in a MVC, 54% were
unrestrained.
Four injury patterns are common in children with cervical spine trauma: fracture,
fracture with subluxation, subluxation without fracture, and SCIWORA. Isolated soft-
tissue injuries above C3 tend to occur in younger children, whereas children aged 11
years or older sustain fracture with or without associated subluxation. Injuries in the
cervical spine typically result from forced a hyperextension injury; axial loading; and/or
an acceleration-deceleration injury involving the head, with forced hyperflexion, such as
that sustained in an MVC.
The deforming forces contributing to injury in the thoracolumbar spine typically include
compression, flexion-distraction, or combined forced vectors. Immature wedged
vertebral bodies have a propensity for compression fractures, whereas tension can

translate through the posterior ligamentous complex (PLC), as in a flexion-distraction
type of injury. Tension also can be translated through the relatively weak physeal
cartilage of the vertebral body, resulting in Salter Harris type I fracture.3 High-energy
torsional, distraction, and/or shearing forces can cause a fracture-dislocation injury in
the thoracolumbar spine, which is a rare but potentially devastating injury greatly
associated with nerve root, spinal cord, and/or cauda equina injury.
Associated Injuries
40% to 65% of patients with spinal trauma have associated injuries.4,5
The most frequent associated injuries include abdominal injuries, thoracic injuries, head
injuries, and long bone fractures.
Chance fractures are greatly associated with intraabdominal injuries.

Associated Injuries
In a multicenter study of level 1 trauma centers evaluating associated injuries in 332
children and adolescents with spinal trauma, Rush et al5 reported that 62% of patients
sustained associated injuries, including 57% of patients aged 0 to 3 years, 52% of
patients aged 4 to 12 years, and 64% of patients aged 13 to 19 years. Thoracic injuries,
including pulmonary contusion, pneumothorax, and rib fracture, were the most
common injuries, occurring in 37% of patients, followed by abdominal injuries in 25% of
patients, head injuries in 23% of patients, and skeletal injuries in 21% of patients. Injury
distribution was similar among all age groups. In patients aged 3 years or younger, the
associated injury rate was 57%, with facial and/or head trauma occurring in 36% of
patients. Associated traumatic brain injury in 37% of younger patients resulted in a
mortality rate of 50%.5
In the thoracolumbar spine, the risk of abdominal and thoracic visceral injuries is higher
in pediatric patients compared with adults because of underdeveloped protective ribs,
iliac crest, and musculature. The incidence of abdominal and thoracic visceral injurie is
especially high with flexion-distraction (Chance) fractures, which are associated with a
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000579
9/80

70% risk of abdominal injury.5 The seat belt sign is transverse abdominal bruising
secondary to a lap belt restraint and may be indicative of abdominal and/or
thoracolumbar spine injury because abdominal flexion over a lap seat belt causes
compression of visceral structures. Common associated injuries include small bowel
injuries, pancreatic rupture, hemothorax, pneumothorax, lung contusion, and aortic
injury.
Injury Prevention
More than 50% of patients who sustain an injury in a MVC are unrestrained or improperly
restrained.
The American Academy of Pediatrics has issued seat belt and child safety seat policies, which
are endorsed by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS).15
Recommendations to promote safer ATV practices also have been made by the AAOS.

Injury Prevention
MVCs are the most common cause of spine injury in pediatric patients and the leading
cause of death in children. More than 5,000 children and adolescents die in MVCs each
year, and for every fatality, more than 400 pediatric patients undergo medical treatment
for injuries sustained in a MVC.15 Of patients who sustain an injury in a MVC, 50% to 68%
are unrestrained or improperly restrained.5,6
The American Academy of Pediatrics has issued seat belt and child safety seat policies,15
which have been endorsed by AAOS. These policies state the following: (1) all infants and
toddlers should ride in a rear-facing car seat until they are aged 2 years or the highest
weight/height allowed by the car seat manufacturer; (2) all children aged 2 years or older
or who have outgrown the rear-facing weight/height limit for their car seat, should use a
forward-facing car seat with a harness for as long as possible; (3) all children with a
weight/height that exceeds the forward-facing car seat limit should use a belt-positioning
booster seat until the vehicle lap-and-shoulder seat belt fits properly, typically by the
time a child has reached 4 feet 9 inches and is aged 8 to 12 years; (4) if children are old

lap-and-shoulder seat belt for optimal protection; and (5) children younger than 13 years
should be restrained in the rear seats of a vehicle for optimal protection.
Thoracolumbar spine trauma from ATV use has been rapidly increasing in children
younger than 16 years. Recommendations to promote safer ATV practices have been
made by the AAOS.16 ATVs should never be driven by children younger than 12 years,
and limitations on ATV use with supervision should be enforced for children younger
than 16 years.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Overview
Initial management—Patients should be evaluated and treated according to Advanced Trauma
Life Support (ATLS) protocol for children.
Accommodate pediatric patients’ large head: body ratio on backboard
Early recognition and management of SCI is critical to improving outcomes.

Overview
Pediatric patients should be transported on a backboard with a pediatric cutout for the
occiput or on a standard backboard with pads to elevate the torso to prevent
inadvertent flexion or kyphosis of the cervical spine resulting from the child’s
disproportionately large head size.17 A hard cervical collar should be placed, and spinal
immobilization via log roll precautions should be maintained until the injury is evaluated.
In patients with SCI, avoid hypotension and hypoxia. Systolic blood pressure greater than
90 mm Hg and oxygen saturation of 100% should be maintained to improve neurologic
outcomes. Hypotension may result from hypovolemic shock because of blood loss from
abdominal or pelvic injury or from neurogenic shock, which results from disruption of
sympathetic tone as a result of SCI. Neurogenic shock leads to vasodilatation and

spinal shock is a physiologic response to trauma with transient flaccid paralysis and
areflexia, including absence of the bulbocavernosus reflex.
Patient History
Mechanism of injury
Symptoms: neurologic changes, neck pain, back pain, head/facial pain, abdominal pain
In children aged 3 years or younger, a high index of suspicion for nonaccidental trauma should
be maintained.

Patient History
A high index of suspicion for spinal injury should be maintained during evaluation of a
trauma patient. The patient history should focus on understanding the mechanism of
injury, such as a MVC, a fall from greater than body height, bicycling or diving injury,
forced hyperextension injury, or acceleration-deceleration injury involving the head. For
MVCs, focus on understanding the type of collision, speed, location of impact and
location in car, and presence and type of restraint (forward-/rear-facing car seat, lap belt
and/or shoulder belt) to guide appropriate suspicion for specific injury patterns.
Signs and symptoms that should prompt immobilization and imaging studies include
neck pain, back pain, focal neck and/or back tenderness to palpation, unconsciousness,
inability to assess the back because of a distracting injury, abnormal neurologic
examination, history of neurologic symptoms, physical signs of trauma (ecchymosis,
abrasion, deformity, swelling, tenderness), unreliable examination secondary to
substance abuse, considerable face/head trauma, abnormal head positioning (ie,
torticollis), or inconsolability. In addition, a medical, surgical, family, and social history,
including baseline developmental status and/or disability and/or preexisting
musculoskeletal conditions, should be obtained.

A high index of suspicion for nonaccidental trauma should be maintained in children
aged 3 years or younger, with special attention focused on fractures in a nonambulatory
child, bruising, skull fractures/head injury, delayed presentation, prior emergency
department visits, unwitnessed injury, burns, chronic medical conditions, physical
examination or radiographic findings inconsistent with the patient history, and/or any
unusual behavior of the child or caregivers.19
Physical Examination
The initial physical examination should follow Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol, with
assessment of the airway, breathing, and circulation.
The neurologic examination should be performed according to the American Spine Injury
Association (ASIA) classification system.

Physical Examination
The initial physical examination follows Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol, with
assessment of the airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. A patient with
a potential spinal injury is protected in a cervical collar during evaluation; the cervical
collar is removed only for physical examination and skin care until the cervical spine is
cleared. If the patient is log rolled, the entire spine should be evaluated for physical signs
of trauma, including ecchymosis, abrasion, deformity, contusion, swelling, and open
injuries. The entire spine also should be palpated for tenderness, step-off, crepitus, or
open injuries. The face/head, thorax, and abdomen should be examined for associated
injuries, such as abdominal bruising from a lap seat belt (seat belt sign).
A detailed neurologic examination should be performed, including objective scoring of
mental status using the Pediatric Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). The ASIA International
Standards for Neurological Classification of SCI (Resource 4) should be determined via a
motor examination by upper and lower extremity myotomes, a sensory examination
with light touch and pinprick by dermatome, and an anorectal examination to evaluate
for the presence of spinal shock. During the anorectal examination (if appropriate), the
external anal sphincter is assessed for voluntary motor and sensory function, and the

bulbocavernosus reflex is assessed (tugging on urinary catheter elicits internal and
external anal sphincter contraction).20 After spinal shock has resolved, as evidenced by
return of the bulbocavernosus reflex, patients are classified as ASIA grade A through E.
Complete injury (ASIA grade A) involves absence of all motor and sensory function distal
to the injury, including the sacral segments. ASIA grade B involves absent motor function
but intact sensation. ASIA grade C involves motor function of less than 3/5 in more than
one-half of the muscles below the neurologic level of injury. ASIA grade D involves motor
function of more than 3/5 in more than one-half of the muscles below the neurologic
level of injury. ASIA grade E involves normal motor and sensory function. The neurologic
level of injury is defined as the most caudal segment with intact sensation and
antigravity (3/5) motor function.20
Cervical Spine Clearance
Pediatric Cervical Spine Clearance Working Group algorithm21

Cervical Spine Clearance
The Pediatric Cervical Spine Working Group recently developed standardized guidelines
for evidence-based pediatric cervical spine clearance (Resource 5; Figure 2). In patients
with intact mental function (GCS score of 14 or 15), the cervical spine can be cleared if no
signs or symptoms of cervical spine injury, including persistent neck pain, difficulty with
neck movement, focal sensory abnormality or motor deficit, torticollis or abnormal head
position, posterior midline neck tenderness, and distracting injury, are present and
cervical range of motion is normal. If clinical clearance is not possible, initial radiographic
evaluation consists of a single lateral radiograph of the cervical spine. Patients may be
placed in a rigid cervical collar and undergo re-evaluation in 1 to 2 weeks and/or flexion-
extension radiographs (=30° flexion and =30° extension) can be obtained for
clearance.21
In patients with a GCS score of 9 to 13, a lateral radiograph remains the preferred initial
imaging modality if potential to improve to a GCS score of 14 to 15 exists. A CT scan is

Cervical Spine Radiography

Cervical spine: initial radiographic evaluation is a lateral radiograph.
Physiologic variants in pediatric patients, such as pseudosubluxation, which is present in 20%
to 40% of pediatric patients, often are confused with injury.
The atlanto-dens interval (ADI) normally is 5 mm or less in pediatric patients.

Cervical Spine Radiography
Initial radiographic evaluation for a suspected injury is a lateral radiograph of the cervical
spine. Visualization of the C7 through T1 junction on a lateral radiograph is cruciate. An
odontoid view typically is unnecessary in young pediatric patients aged 8 years or
younger because it typically does not aid in diagnosis.22
Interpretation of cervical spine radiographs often is a challenge in pediatric patients
because of developing anatomy. Pseudosubluxation is a physiologic variant present in
20% to 40% of pediatric patients; this is most commonly observed at C2-3 but also is
observed at C3-4. It can be differentiated from injury by evaluating the spinolaminar line
(Swischuk line) along the posterior arch from C1 to C3; step-off greater than 1.5 mm is
concerning for true injury (Figure 3). Normal growth centers, such as the dentocentral
synchondrosis; secondary centers of ossification of the spinous processes; and/or
unfused ring apophyses may be misinterpreted as fractures. Other normal variants in
pediatric patients include loss of cervical lordosis with the neck in a neutral position,
such as in a rigid collar, and physiologic anterior vertebral body wedging of 3 mm or less;
however, angulation of vertebral levels caudal to C4, especially if greater than 11°, may
represent spine injury in children aged 8 years or older.
Atlantoaxial instability (AAI) is evaluated via the ADI. An ADI greater than 5 mm in
children and greater than 3 mm in adolescents/adults is abnormal. If the ADI is greater
than 10 mm, all ligaments have failed, creating cord compression from loss of space
available for the spinal cord.
On a lateral radiograph, the retropharyngeal space should be less than 6 mm at C2 and
less than 22 mm at C6. These spaces may be enlarged in children because of crying;
therefore, enlargement is not necessarily a sign of underlying injury in children.

Thoracolumbar Spine Radiography
AP and lateral plain radiographs are favored for initial imaging in patients with a history,
mechanism of injury, and physical examination suggestive of thoracolumbar spine injury.
In patients with a diagnosed spinal injury, plain radiographs of the entire spine are necessary
because of a risk of multilevel injury.


Thoracolumbar Spine Radiography
AP and lateral plain radiographs are favored for initial imaging of suspected
thoracolumbar spine injury; however, no evidence-based guidelines are available for

required. In patients with a diagnosed spinal injury, plain radiographs of the entire spine

Overview
Many cervical spine fractures can be managed nonsurgically in pediatric patients. Some
indications for nonsurgical management include SCIWORA, AAI associated with an
avulsion fracture, odontoid synchondrosis fractures that can be satisfactorily reduced via
extension, Jefferson fractures without AAI, and Hangman fractures without ligamentous
instability or facet dislocation. Nonsurgical management typically consists of halo vest
immobilization for 6 to 12 weeks, depending on the injury type. Advanced imaging
studies and/or assessment of dynamic stability to evaluate healing typically is performed
at time of transition out of the halo vest.
Cervical Orthoses
Rigid cervical collars can be used to manage stable fractures of the upper or middle cervical
spine.
Minerva casts/cervicothoracic orthoses can be used to stabilize the subaxial cervical spine and
the cervicothoracic junction.
A halo vest is the preferred method for immobilization of unstable injuries of the upper
cervical spine; however, halo vest immobilization is associated with a 39% rate of major pin-
related complications.
Pinless halo vest systems are a viable treatment option for pediatric patients to avoid pin-
related complications.

Several anatomic features of the cervical spine make rigid immobilization of this region a
challenge. Soft cervical collars have little effect on restricting motion but can be used to
manage whiplash injuries or neck pain without unstable bony or ligamentous injury.
Rigid cervical collars are most effective in the middle cervical spine but also are the
preferred option for the management of stable fractures of the upper cervical spine.65
The addition of a thoracic extension to a rigid cervical collar provides more effective
immobilization of the subaxial cervical spine and the cervicothoracic junction. If more
rigid immobilization is necessary, a Minerva cast is a cervicothoracic orthosis that
extends farther down the trunk and can be used for injuries caudally to approximately
T5.65 Some disagreement exists with regard to the extent to which a Minerva cast
immobilizes the upper cervical spine, with some studies advocating the use of a Minerva
cast for fractures below C2.66 Minerva casts were originally described as a plaster cast
jacket. Currently, prefabricated Minerva body jackets are available; however, Minerva
cast immobilization remains a viable treatment option for pediatric patients.
Although a halo vest has been considered the best immobilization method for unstable
injuries of the upper cervical spine (occiput through C2), major halo vest–related
complications have been reported in as many as 39% of children, including infection,
loosening, skull penetration, scarring, and risk of severe intracranial injury with falls.67
Skull thickness in children younger than 6 years is highly variable (range, 1.1 to 4.3 mm),
which may increase the risk of inner skull penetration.68 Noninvasive halo vest systems
can be used to stabilize the upper cervical spine while avoiding pin-related complications
and may be a compromise between a halo vest and a Minerva cast. Noninvasive halo
vest systems have been shown to be effective for odontoid fracture, C1-C2 rotatory
subluxation, congenital muscular torticollis, and postoperative immobilization in

Many upper cervical spine fractures can be managed with the use of a halo vest for
external immobilization. Children require a greater number of pins and less insertional
torque than adults because of a relatively thin calvarium with open sutures. Eight to 12
pins should be placed at torques of 2 to 4 in/lb in young children (versus four pins
tightened to 8 in/lb in adults). The age at which pediatric patients can be treated via a
traditional four-pin halo vest has not been firmly established; however, such treatment
typically is safe after age 11 years.70 The ring should be less than1 cm away from the
skin because a large ring is predisposed to loosening from greater cantilever bending.
The anterolateral pins should be placed into the safe zone, which is 1 cm above the
lateral one-third of the orbit, just above the pinna, at or below the equator of the skull70

medial to the thin temporal bone and temporalis muscle. The posterolateral pins have a
wider safe zone, which is below the skull equator, approximately diagonal to the
contralateral anterolateral pin, parallel to the transverse plane of the head.

Thoracolumbar Spine Injuries
Most thoracolumbar spine fractures can be managed nonsurgically, including
compression fractures, SCIWORA, transverse and spinous process fractures, burst
fractures (if neurologically intact without considerable deformity [ie, kyphosis <30°]), and
osseous Chance fractures (if neurologically intact without considerable posterior
ligament disruption or deformity).
Nonsurgical management depends on the fracture pattern. Stable injuries, such as
transverse and spinous process fractures, can be managed symptomatically via pain
control, whereas most compression fractures also can be managed symptomatically via
activity restrictions for at least 6 weeks. Higher energy injuries with increased osseous
involvement, such as burst fractures and osseous Chance fractures, can be managed
with the use of a TLSO for 8 to 12 weeks.

Indications
Nonsurgical management of unstable injuries in pediatric patients frequently fails.57 In
the cervical spine, ligamentous injuries typically require surgical stabilization. Indications
include atlanto-occipital instability, AAI with an ADI that exceeds 5 mm, odontoid
fractures displaced more than 100% that cannot be reduced, Jefferson or Hangman
fractures with ligamentous instability or facet dislocation, and unstable subaxial cervical
spine injuries (especially with an associated neurologic deficit).

require surgical stabilization, especially in patients with ligamentous involvement or a
neurologic deficit. Distraction and shear injuries with displacement, flexion-distraction
injures that are purely ligamentous injuries, bony injuries with more than 20° to 30° of
kyphosis, associated neurologic injuries, and/or polytrauma patients who cannot
tolerate brace or cast immobilization also typically require surgical stabilization.

Cervical Spine Injuries
Traditionally, wiring techniques were used for cervical fixation in young pediatric patients
followed by a halo vest orthosis; however, these wiring techniques were found to be
associated with a high rate of nonunion because they are inherently less stable than
rigid screw constructs in all planes of flexion-extension, lateral bending, and lateral
rotation.72
The development of small cervical pedicle and lateral mass screws has facilitated surgical
stabilization in pediatric patients, resulting in higher rates of union. Posterior cervical
screws have been approved by the FDA for any patient, regardless of age, with an
osseous structure that is dimensionally adequate to accommodate posterior screw
placement. Retrospective studies of pediatric patients support the safety and efficacy of
screws, with satisfactory fusion rates and low complication rates.73-75
Biomechanical analyses, CT studies, and some retrospective reviews have reported that
occiput keel screws, C1 lateral mass screws, C1-2 trans-articular screws, C2 pars/pedicle
screws, C2 laminar screws, and subaxial lateral mass screws may be safe in some
pediatric patients depending on anatomic size constraints; therefore, preoperative CT
scan and/or intraoperative navigation systems are essential for safe screw placement in
pediatric patients.76-78
Rigid fixation for the management of unstable cervical spine injuries in pediatric patients
follows principles, approaches, techniques, and complications similar to those in adult
patients. Craniocervical instability is managed via occiput to C2 fusion followed by halo
vest stabilization, preferably with rigid internal fixation. AAI necessitates C1-C2 posterior

Thoracolumbar Spine Injuries
Although limited data is available on surgical techniques for the management of
pediatric spine injuries, robust literature is available on surgical techniques in the adult
population, and extensive data support safe and effective use of spinal instrumentation
for the management of pediatric spinal deformity. In general, pediatric patients have
high rates of union after undergoing instrumented spinal fusion performed via
techniques similar to those used in adults with a spinal injury.3,79,80 The need for
concomitant decompression is based on neurologic compromise and the amount of
neural element compression. Indirect canal decompression is accomplished via surgical
distraction of the injured level. Direct decompression may be indicated for neurologic
deficits.4
Posterior instrumentation and fusion of unstable thoracolumbar fractures is the
preferred treatment option for most flexion-distraction injuries (Figure 14, D) and some
burst fractures. No consensus exists on level selection because a balance exists between
motion segment preservation and the stability of fixation. In general, injuries typically
require instrumentation one or two levels above and below the fracture. Thoracic-level
fusions tend to be longer than lumbar fusions because less concern exists for preserving
mobility and, therefore, the primary objective is stability. Fusions also tend to be longer if
decompression is performed.

typically does not remodel and may worsen), pseudarthrosis, implant failure, neurologic injury,
